cards.title: SMS list growth via optimized pop-ups and opt-in placement
cards.summary: Grow an SMS subscriber list by treating pop-ups, checkout opt-ins, and conversational touchpoints as deliberate opt-in surfaces rather than afterthoughts.
cards.use_when: You need to build or accelerate SMS list growth for an ecommerce store before SMS flows and campaigns can drive revenue.
steps: Audit every existing opt-in surface on your store — homepage pop-up, exit-intent, checkout, post-purchase, account pages — and identify where SMS consent is currently offered versus email-only.
Add SMS as an explicit opt-in option within email signup pop-ups and checkout, rather than a separate uncoordinated pop-up, so consent feels like one native signup experience.

Optimize pop-up copy and incentive for the SMS channel specifically: state clearly what subscribers will receive (offers, drops, order updates) and the expected message frequency, since SMS consent is more sensitive than email.
Test opt-in placement and timing (immediate vs exit-intent vs scroll-triggered) and measure opt-in rate per surface, not just total list size.
Use conversational commerce touchpoints — the same SMS thread that welcomes new subscribers — to collect zero-party data (preferences, sizes, interests) that informs segmentation and personalization.
caveats: SMS opt-in regulations (TCPA and similar) require explicit consent and frequency disclosure; verify current compliance requirements for your markets before scaling.
Pop-up and opt-in best practices and platform interfaces change frequently — verify the current tool interface before implementing.

cards.title: Using conversational commerce to overcome mid-funnel objections
cards.summary: Treat SMS as a two-way conversational channel that resolves mid-funnel purchase hesitation, not as a one-way blast channel.
cards.use_when: Prospects or subscribers are stalling mid-funnel — browsing, adding to cart, or asking questions — and you need a channel to handle objections before purchase.
steps: Identify the objections that stall buyers mid-funnel (fit, compatibility, shipping, price/value, timing) and map which ones can be resolved in a short text exchange rather than a long email.
Design SMS flows that invite a reply rather than only broadcasting — e.g., a browse-abandon or cart-abandon message that asks a specific question and offers human or AI-assisted help.
Use the reply thread to answer the objection directly and, where relevant, to collect zero-party data (preferences, intent, constraints) that improves subsequent targeting.
Route qualified conversations toward the purchase decision with a link or offer, and route unresolved or complex cases to a human agent where possible.
Measure conversational SMS by reply rate and downstream purchase conversion, not just click-through, since the channel's value is in the dialogue.
caveats: SMS conversational commerce depends on staffing or automation to respond; unanswered threads can damage trust more than no message.
The source describes strategy and rationale, not tested conversion benchmarks — treat any performance expectations as hypotheses to validate in your own store.

cards.title: Defining SMS campaign frequency and cadence
cards.summary: Set a deliberate SMS send frequency that balances revenue opportunity against subscriber tolerance and opt-out risk.
cards.use_when: You are planning how often to send SMS campaigns to an ecommerce list without driving unsubscribes or complaints.
steps: Decide the intended role of SMS relative to email — for example, high-urgency, time-sensitive sends (drops, flash sales, order/shipping updates) versus a parallel promotional channel.
Set an explicit monthly or weekly send cap per subscriber and document it, then hold campaigns to that cap rather than sending whenever a promotion appears.
Segment the list so frequency can vary by engagement and consent type — recent buyers and high-intent subscribers can typically tolerate more messages than cold or inactive subscribers.
Review opt-out rate and reply sentiment after each send window and adjust cadence; a rising opt-out rate is the clearest signal to reduce frequency.
Coordinate SMS and email calendars so subscribers do not receive near-duplicate promotions across both channels in the same short window.
caveats: Compliance rules and platform guidance on frequency vary by region and carrier; verify current requirements before setting caps.
The source frames frequency as a strategic decision rather than a fixed number — do not assume a universal optimal cadence.

cards.title: Segmenting SMS subscribers for relevance
cards.summary: Apply the same segmentation discipline to SMS as to email so texts stay relevant and opt-out risk stays low.
cards.use_when: You are building SMS flows or campaigns and need to decide which subscribers receive which messages.
steps: Segment SMS subscribers by engagement and lifecycle stage — new opt-in, active buyer, lapsed, VIP — and by the zero-party data collected through signup and conversational replies.
Build SMS flows that mirror the core lifecycle moments (welcome, browse/cart abandonment, post-purchase, win-back) and tailor copy per segment rather than sending one broadcast to the whole list.
Use conversational replies to enrich segments over time, since SMS naturally produces preference and intent signals that email cannot easily capture.
Suppress or reduce frequency for low-engagement segments to protect deliverability and list health, and re-engage them with a distinct offer before removing them.
Report results at segment level so you can see which segments justify SMS investment and which should stay email-only.
caveats: Segmentation granularity is limited by the data you actually collected at opt-in or through replies; do not assume demographic data you never asked for.
SMS and email platform segmentation features change — verify current capability in your tool.

cards.title: Building core automated SMS flows
cards.summary: Map SMS automation to the same core lifecycle flows used in email, prioritizing moments where texting beats email for urgency or immediacy.
cards.use_when: You are setting up or expanding automated SMS flows for an ecommerce store and need to decide which flows to build first.
steps: Start from the core lifecycle flow set (welcome, browse abandonment, cart abandonment, post-purchase, win-back) and assess each for whether SMS adds value over email — typically where urgency, immediacy, or a quick reply matters.
For cart and browse abandonment, use SMS for short, timely nudges and keep the message conversational so the subscriber can reply with questions.
For post-purchase, use SMS for shipping and delivery updates plus a light retention follow-up, since transactional texts have high attention and low opt-out risk when expected.
For welcome flows, use the first text to set frequency expectations and collect a preference or zero-party data point in the reply thread.
For win-back, test SMS re-engagement separately from email and compare reactivation and opt-out rates before committing budget.
caveats: The source is strategy-level and does not provide tested flow-level conversion benchmarks; validate flow performance in your own account.
Message content and automation features differ by SMS platform — verify current interface and compliance settings before launch.
